newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul shrs end down on fundamentals, not labour law.
newsitem.headline: Seoul shrs end down on fundamentals, not labour law.

text.p: Seoul stocks ended Tuesday's trading sharply lower, pressured by rising interest rates, a weakening won, and other poor fundamentals, brokers said.
The collapse of support at the 660-level helped accelerate selling. The passage of a new labour law on Monday barely made an impression, they added.
The composite stock index fell 11.40 points to close at 655.95. Declining shares eclipsed gainers 667 to 177.
"The major factors are the bond rates and the weakening foreign exchange rates," said Kim Se-jung of Dongwon Securities.

South Korea's parliament passed a new labour bill on Monday, replacing a law that sparked nearly a month of strikes. The new legislation delays for two years implementation of a controversial clause making it easier for companies to lay off workers.
Brokers said the index could see a slight technical rebound on Wednesday, as it has declined for three consecutive days.

Rising interest rates are sapping strength from the stock market, brokers said. Bond yields have been rising on fear of a liquidity squeeze. Benchmark three-year bonds were trading at a year high of 12.70 percent near the end of Tuesday's trading.
Foreigners have also shied away from the market because of the falling won/dollar exchange rate, they said.
The won, which was trading at around 879 in late trading, has declined by about four percent since the beginning of the year.
Brokers said that news that the Federation of Korean Industries may intervene in a hostile takeover bid for Midopa sent related stocks tumbling.
Dainong shot back to the top the most actives list, falling 370 won to 7,730.
Dainong is the parent firm of Midopa, which has been targetted for a takeover by Shindongbang. Shindongbang fell 400 won to 37,000, while Midopa lost 2,800 to its lower limit of 32,400.
Investors were still hopeful that the government would raise the foreign shareholding ceiling or ease the real-name financial transaction system, brokers said.
Foreigners will be allowed to buy up to 23 percent of most stocks some time this year, up from 20 percent. A schedule has not yet been set.

Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik said last week that he felt the real-name system, which bans the use of false name accounts for all financial transactions, needed improvements. This led to speculation that regulations would be eased, bringing black market funds into the stock market.
Many heavily index-weighted large cap shares fell throughout the day. Dacom lost 4,000 won to 103,000, and POSCO shed 1,000 won to 40,200.
